literal.prompt: Кто первым венчался на царство как царь всея Руси?

literalGroups.primaryGround: The museum states that the 1547 Ivan IV coronation was the event at which the tsar and autocrat titles were first officially adopted (L149); L137 distinguishes an earlier Grand-Prince enthronement for Dmitry, so “царь всея Руси” uniquely points to Ivan IV.
literalGroups.locator: Музеи Московского Кремля, История собора L137,L149,L151

literalGroups.literal: Иван IV венчался на царство в 1547 году. В истории он широко известен как Иван Грозный.
literalGroups.primaryGround: The page labels the ceremony “Венчание на царство Ивана Грозного” (L142,L146) and identifies Ivan IV at L149; L149 gives the 16 January 1547 date.

literalGroups.literal: Иван IV венчался на царство в 1547 году.
literalGroups.primaryGround: Ivan IV’s coronation occurred on 16 January 1547 in the Assumption Cathedral (L149).
The page states that in 1721 Tsar Peter I accepted the emperor title, proclaimed Russia an empire, and introduced coronation (L151), supporting the note about his imperial title.

literalGroups.literal: Александр Невский — новгородский князь XIII века, связанный с Невской битвой и Ледовым побоищем.
literalGroups.primaryGround: The Library identifies Alexander as Novgorod grand prince (1236–1251) at L44; L46 recounts the 1240 victory on the Neva and L49 the 1242 Ice Battle.

literalGroups.literal: Николай II — последний российский император, отрёкшийся от престола в 1917 году.
literalGroups.primaryGround: The PDF is explicitly an exhibition on Nicholas II (P0 L0-L2); its P19-P20 L408-L421 says the last Russian emperor signed the abdication act in March 1917 and names Nicholas II in the passage/caption.

fourFullPromptAnswerNoteAssessments.fullPrompt: Кто первым венчался на царство как царь всея Руси?
fourFullPromptAnswerNoteAssessments.note: Иван IV венчался на царство в 1547 году.
fourFullPromptAnswerNoteAssessments.grammar: “Кто первым венчался...” is answered naturally by a nominative personal name; “Иван IV” is the established Russian form.
fourFullPromptAnswerNoteAssessments.plausibilityUniqueKeyAndNoteTruthUsefuln: Ivan IV is the unique key: the Kremlin museum states his 1547 ceremony was the first formal acceptance of the tsar/autocrat titles (L149). Peter I adopted the later imperial title (L151); Alexander Nevsky was a 13th-century Novgorod prince (PBL L44); Nicholas II was the last emperor (PBL P19-P20 L408-L421). All four are plausible Russian rulers, but only Ivan IV fits the “first tsar” relation. The correct note adds the date.
